::: {.callout-note}
## How Gym days work
1. Learn **one pattern** (today: hash-map lookup)
2. Solve problems with the **4-step method**
3. Every problem solved **twice** — R and Python — because idiom-building is the point

Gym problems are small on purpose. Struggle 10–15 minutes before peeking.
LeetCode-tier interviews mostly ask easy/medium array-string problems; this
track gets you there in four weeks.
:::

## The 4-step method (use it forever)

1. **Restate** the problem in one sentence, define inputs/outputs
2. **Brute force** it out loud — "nested loops, O(n²)"
3. **Name the bottleneck** — usually "I keep re-searching a list"
4. **Reach for a hash map** — trading memory for instant lookup, O(n)

Worked application, Two-Sum: *restate — find two values summing to target;
brute force — every pair i<j, O(n²); bottleneck — for each x I re-scan the
array asking "is target−x here?"; hash map — remember everything seen so
far, ask the map instead of the array. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.*
That paragraph is the thinking; the code below is just transcription.

## Big-O in 90 seconds

| Big-O | Name | Feel | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | "regardless of size" | `d[key]` dict lookup |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | "halving" | binary search |
| O(n) | linear | "touch each item once" | one loop |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | "sort-ish" | sorting |
| O(n²) | quadratic | "every pair" | nested loops over same data |

Rules of thumb: nested loops over the same n → multiply (`n²`).
Sequential loops → add (`O(n + n) = O(n)`). Sorting is n log n.
**Big-O describes growth, not seconds** — an O(n²) over n=10 beats an O(n)
over n=10 million any day; know your n (scRNA-seq: n = tens of thousands of
cells × tens of thousands of genes — O(n²) cell-pair loops are why
naive clustering code crashes).

## Reading complexity: the real interview skill

```r
# a) O(n)  — one pass
total <- 0; for (v in x) total <- total + v

# b) O(n²) — for each element, re-scan everything
for (i in seq_along(x)) for (j in seq_along(x)) check(x[i], x[j])

# c) O(n log n) — sort then one pass
o <- order(x); check_pairs(x[o])

# d) O(n) inside O(n) = O(n²) disguised: %in% inside a loop!
for (v in xs) if (v %in% big) hit()      # %in% is a full scan each time
```

That last one is the most common **bioinformatics R performance bug**:
`%in%`/`match()` inside a loop over thousands of genes. Pull the loop
inside-out — one vectorized `match(all_genes, wanted)` — and it's O(n).

## R's hash tools (no dict literal, same idea)

R has no `{}` dict, but these are all hash-backed:

| Tool | Job |
|---|---|
| `match(x, table)` | first position of each `x` in `table` |
| `%in%` | membership → TRUE/FALSE |
| `anyDuplicated(x)` | >0 means "has a duplicate" — stops early! |
| `unique(x)`, `duplicated(x)` | dedupe / mark 2nd+ occurrences |
| `table(x)` | counts (like Python `Counter`) |
| named vector `setNames(v, n)` | lookup by name via `v[name]` |

Python equivalents: `dict`, `set`, `collections.Counter`, `in`.

## Problem 1 — Two-Sum (the classic)

> Given `nums` and `target`, return the two numbers that add to `target`.

The map holds **values seen so far → their positions**. Check for the
partner *before* inserting today's value — that ordering is what makes
duplicates and "don't pair with yourself" work out.

```{webr}
#| label: twosum-r
two_sum <- function(nums, target) {
  seen <- integer(0)                    # named hash: value -> position
  for (i in seq_along(nums)) {
    partner <- target - nums[i]
    if (partner %in% names(seen)) {
      return(c(nums[seen[[as.character(partner)]]], nums[i]))
    }
    seen[[as.character(nums[i])]] <- i  # add AFTER checking
  }
  NULL
}

two_sum(c(4, 7, 11, 2, 15), 18)
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: twosum-py
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> position
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [nums[seen[target - x]], x]
        seen[x] = i
    return None

print(two_sum([4, 7, 11, 2, 15], 18))
```

Both O(n) time, O(n) space. **The pattern: walk once, ask the hash map for
the partner you need.**

## Problem 2 — Contains Duplicate

> Return TRUE if any value appears twice.

```{webr}
#| label: dup-r
has_duplicate <- function(x) anyDuplicated(x) > 0

has_duplicate(c(1, 2, 3, 2))   # TRUE — stops at the first dup
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: dup-py
def has_duplicate(x):
    return len(set(x)) < len(x)

print(has_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 2]))    # True
```

Two idioms, same O(n). Note what you'd NOT write: `sum(duplicated(x)) > 0`
is fine, but `for i, for j, x[i]==x[j]` is the O(n²) reflex we're un-training.

## Problem 3 — First Recurring Character

```{webr}
#| label: recur-r
first_recurring <- function(s) {
  chars <- strsplit(s, "")[[1]]
  dup_idx <- which(duplicated(chars))
  if (length(dup_idx) == 0) NULL else chars[dup_idx[1]]
}

first_recurring("abba")     # "b" — b repeats at position 3, before a's repeat
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: recur-py
def first_recurring(s):
    seen = set()
    for ch in s:
        if ch in seen:
            return ch
        seen.add(ch)
    return None

print(first_recurring("abba"))    # 'b' — it recurs at position 3, before 'a' repeats
```

Same answer by different machinery: R marks duplicates in one vectorized
pass then reports the earliest; Python walks once with a set. Compare the
*shapes* — R thinks in whole-vector operations, Python in an explicit loop.

## Problem 4 — Valid Anagram (count, don't sort)

> Same letters, same counts? Sorting works (O(n log n)) but counting is O(n).

```{webr}
#| label: anagram-r
is_anagram <- function(a, b) {
  all(table(strsplit(tolower(a), "")[[1]]) ==
      table(strsplit(tolower(b), "")[[1]]))
}

is_anagram("Listen", "Silent")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: anagram-py
from collections import Counter

def is_anagram(a, b):
    return Counter(a.lower()) == Counter(b.lower())

print(is_anagram("Listen", "Silent"))
print(Counter("mississippi"))           # the full count table
print(Counter("mississippi")["z"])      # missing keys are FREE (0, not NA)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Counter's superpower R's table lacks
`Counter("abc")["z"]` returns `0` — missing keys are free.
R's `table()["z"]` returns `NA`. Counting problems in R need the extra
guard: `if ("z" %in% names(freq))`.
:::

## Problem 5 — Missing Number

> `0..n` with one missing, find it. Math beats any data structure: expected
> sum minus actual sum. O(n) time, O(1) space.

```{webr}
#| label: missing-r
missing_number <- function(nums) {
  n <- length(nums)                      # one value missing from 0..n
  n * (n + 1) / 2 - sum(nums)
}

missing_number(c(0, 1, 3, 4, 5))
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: missing-py
def missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(nums)

print(missing_number([0, 1, 3, 4, 5]))    # 2
```

Lesson: the *fourth* step of the method isn't always a hash map — it's "is
there a mathematical identity that replaces the search?" Sums, products,
XOR (for the bitwise-inclined), counting sort.

## Problem 6 — Best Time to Buy & Sell (one-pass max)

> One array of daily prices, one buy then one later sell — maximize profit.

Brute force: every pair, O(n²). Insight: the best sell for each day pairs
with the *cheapest day before it* — so track `min_so_far` and the best
`profit` in a single pass. O(n).

```{webr}
#| label: profit-r
max_profit <- function(prices) {
  best <- 0
  min_so_far <- prices[1]
  for (p in prices[-1]) {
    best <- max(best, p - min_so_far)
    min_so_far <- min(min_so_far, p)
  }
  best
}

max_profit(c(7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4))
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: profit-py
def max_profit(prices):
    best = 0
    min_so_far = prices[0]
    for p in prices[1:]:
        best = max(best, p - min_so_far)
        min_so_far = min(min_so_far, p)
    return best

print(max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))    # 5  (buy 1, sell 6)
```

**Running-minimum + best-so-far** is a core pattern; it returns as "kadane's
algorithm" and as fold-change QC logic in genomics.

# 9. missing_number(c(1, 2, 0, 4)) — predict

# 10. A nested loop runs 1000 × 1000 iterations; how many in big-O speak?

# 11. What's O(1) about names(seen) membership but O(n) about x %in% y?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `anyDuplicated(c(3,5,5,1)) > 0`
2. `c("a","x","b") %in% c("x","b","q")` (positions) — or `intersect()`
3. "i" and "s", 4 each
4. `c(3, 7)` — the pair check happens before inserting 3; then 7 finds 3
5. `intersect(c(1,2,2,3), c(2,2,4))`
6. O(n·m) technically (scan y per x), O(n) if y is hashed — R's `%in%` hashes
   the table, so effectively linear in length(x)
7. `8` (buy 2, sell 10) — the later cheap 1 can't pair with an earlier sell
8. `c("a")` — names filtered by counts == 2
9. `3` — n=4 → 4·5/2=10 minus sum(1+2+0+4)=7 → 3
10. O(n²) with n=1000 — a million pair-checks
11. `seen[[name]]` lookups hash the names; `%in%` scans — same symbol, 
    different cost. In R use named vectors/dupes-detection instead of scanning
12. `rev(x)` · `x[length(x):1]` · loop with `x[n - i + 1]`
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
# 1. len(set([3, 5, 5, 1])) < len([3, 5, 5, 1]) — predict, then run

# 2. set([1,2,2,3]) & set([2,2,4]) — set intersection; predict the type & value

# 3. Counter("mississippi").most_common(2) — the top 2 letters

# 4. two_sum([5, 5], 10) — predict BEFORE running (the ordering trap)

# 5. missing_number with the math trick on [3, 0, 1]

# 6. dict lookup cost: why is `if x in seen` O(1) while `if x in list` is O(n)?
#    (write the answer as a comment, then ask me if unsure)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. `True` — the classic dedupe-membership test
2. `{2}` — a set (braces, not list); unique shared values
3. `[('i', 4), ('s', 4)]` — (char, count) tuples, ties in insertion order
4. `[5, 5]` — check-first ordering: when the second 5 arrives, partner 5 is
   already in `seen`, so it pairs correctly and never with itself
5. `2` — n=3 → 3·4/2=6 minus sum(3+0+1)=4 → 2
6. dict/set hashing vs linear scan — the whole point of today's pattern
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — first non-repeating character

Return the first character that appears exactly once ("swiss" → "w").
Count first, then scan counts — not nested loops.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d4-nonrep
first_unique <- function(s) {
  ______
}

first_unique("swiss")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d4-nonrep"}
`table()` the letters, find names with count 1, then `match()` those against
the original letters and take the smallest position.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d4-nonrep"}
```r
first_unique <- function(s) {
  chars <- strsplit(s, "")[[1]]
  counts <- table(chars)
  uniques <- names(counts)[counts == 1]
  if (length(uniques) == 0) return(NULL)
  chars[min(match(uniques, chars))]
}
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — the same, in Python

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d4-nonrep-py
def first_unique(s):
    ______

print(first_unique("swiss"))   # 'w'
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d4-nonrep-py"}
`Counter(s)`, then loop `s` and return the first char with `count == 1`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d4-nonrep-py"}
```python
from collections import Counter

def first_unique(s):
    counts = Counter(s)
    for ch in s:
        if counts[ch] == 1:
            return ch
    return None
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — two-sum that returns positions

Modify `two_sum()` to return the **positions** (1-based in R, 0-based in
Python) instead of the values.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d4-twosum-pos
two_sum_pos <- function(nums, target) {
  ______
}

two_sum_pos(c(4, 7, 11, 2, 15), 18)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d4-twosum-pos"}
Same walk, but `seen` already stores positions — return
`c(seen[[partner]], i)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d4-twosum-pos"}
```r
two_sum_pos <- function(nums, target) {
  seen <- integer(0)
  for (i in seq_along(nums)) {
    partner <- as.character(target - nums[i])
    if (partner %in% names(seen)) {
      return(c(seen[[partner]], i))
    }
    seen[[as.character(nums[i])]] <- i
  }
  NULL
}
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — contains-nearby-duplicate (map + window)

Return TRUE if the same value appears within `k` positions of itself.
("nearby duplicates" — a real sequencing QC question: same barcode twice
within k reads?) Hash map of value → last position; compare gaps.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d4-nearby
contains_nearby <- function(nums, k) {
  ______
}

contains_nearby(c(1, 2, 3, 1), 3)   # TRUE  (gap of 3 <= k)
contains_nearby(c(1, 2, 3, 1), 2)   # FALSE (gap of 3 > k)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d4-nearby"}
Keep `last_pos` as a named hash. For each value: if seen and `i - last <= k`
return TRUE; then update `last_pos`. O(n).
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d4-nearby"}
```r
contains_nearby <- function(nums, k) {
  last_pos <- integer(0)
  for (i in seq_along(nums)) {
    key <- as.character(nums[i])
    if (key %in% names(last_pos) && i - last_pos[[key]] <= k) return(TRUE)
    last_pos[[key]] <- i
  }
  FALSE
}
```
:::

### Exercise 5 — character frequency > 1 (Python)

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d4-freq-py
from collections import Counter

def repeated_chars(s):
    """Return a list of characters appearing 2+ times, in first-appearance order."""
    ______

print(repeated_chars("mississippi"))   # ['i', 's', 'p']
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d4-freq-py"}
Build `Counter(s)`, then walk `s` (not the counter!) and collect chars with
`count >= 2`, skipping already-collected ones — or use a seen-set.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d4-freq-py"}
```python
from collections import Counter

def repeated_chars(s):
    counts = Counter(s)
    out, seen = [], set()
    for ch in s:
        if counts[ch] >= 2 and ch not in seen:
            out.append(ch)
            seen.add(ch)
    return out
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. `%in%` inside loops
`for (g in genes) if (g %in% blacklist)` re-scans `blacklist` per gene —
O(n·m). Vectorize: `genes[genes %in% blacklist]` — one call.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. Check-then-insert ordering in Two-Sum
Insert *before* checking and `[5, 5]` with target 10 "pairs" 5 with itself.
Check partner first, insert after.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. `table()` on missing levels
`table(c("a","b"))["z"]` is `NA`, not 0 — guard with `%in% names(...)`.
Python's `Counter` returns 0; R's `table` returns NA. Neither errors — both
flow silently into your logic.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
# Q1: what prints?
x <- c(3, 1, 3, 2, 1)
names(table(x))[table(x) == max(table(x))]

# Q2: what prints, and what's the complexity?
anyDuplicated(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 3))

# Q3: what prints?
two_sum(c(5, 5), 10)

# Q4: trap — what prints?
length(unique(c(NA, NA, 1)))

# Q5: what prints?
max_profit(c(9, 8, 7, 6))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. `"1" "3"` — both appear twice; table order is by value
2. `5` (position of the first duplicate) — early-stops, so *best case* O(1),
   worst O(n)
3. `5 5` — the check-first ordering makes pairing-with-self impossible: when
   scanning the second 5, partner 5 is already in `seen`
4. `2` — NA counts as a unique value (twice!). Real missing-data bug:
   dedupe should usually run after NA handling
5. `0` — prices only fall, so best stays 0 (never a negative profit)
:::
